sentence: Anxiety is the feeling that comes with worrying about something that could happen.
Mind says that feeling anxious from time to time does not mean a person has a mental health problem.
It can become a problem when a person feels anxious a lot of the time, or for months at a time, or has panic attacks.
Generalised anxiety disorder, often shortened to GAD, is a long-term condition.
A person with GAD feels worried or anxious about many different things, rather than about one particular event.
The worry is hard to control and affects daily life.
There are other anxiety disorders too, such as panic disorder and social phobia, which the NHS lists separately.
note: Search summary blended NHS pages; not attributed to a single page.

sentence: GAD affects both the mind and the body.
The main feature is feeling worried or anxious much of the time in a way that is hard to control.
Psychological symptoms can include restlessness, feeling on edge, irritability and difficulty concentrating.

sentence: Physical symptoms can include trouble sleeping, tiring easily, dizziness and a pounding or fluttering heartbeat known as palpitations.

sentence: Because symptoms vary from person to person, the NHS has a separate page on the signs of an anxiety disorder.
The NHS says the exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, but several factors probably play a part.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes no single origin, with genes, social environment and life experiences all contributing and interacting.
It adds that having a close relative with GAD raises a person's risk, but that no single gene is responsible.
Other things linked with GAD include having another anxiety disorder, depression, or a history of stressful or traumatic experiences.

sentence: NICE guidance describes a stepped approach, starting with identifying and assessing the problem, explaining what GAD is and what treatments exist, and active monitoring.
It says education and monitoring alone can suit people whose distress is mild and who have little difficulty in daily life.
The GP may then talk through the options for help with the person, including self-help, talking therapies and medicines.
Anyone worried about their own symptoms can talk to a GP about them.
note: NHS advises seeing a GP if anxiety affects daily life.

sentence: The NHS says people are usually advised to try psychological treatment before being prescribed medicine.
NICE describes low-intensity options first, such as self-help, guided self-help or group sessions that teach about anxiety.
If these are not enough, it describes higher-intensity treatment: CBT or applied relaxation, or a medicine.
The Royal College of Psychiatrists says CBT helps people test their fears and learn to tolerate anxiety.
The usual first medicine is a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, which is also used for anxiety.
note: NHS, RCPsych and NICE patient guidance; blended.

sentence: NICE says benzodiazepines should not usually be offered, other than briefly during a crisis.
Treatment can take time to work, and symptoms may come back.
Antipsychotic medicines are not to be offered for GAD in primary care.
The NHS suggests self-help such as books, online tools or courses that can be done in a person's own time.
Regular exercise and calming breathing exercises are also recommended.
NHS Every Mind Matters suggests mindfulness, and setting aside a daily time for worries if worry takes over the day.
It also says that avoiding situations can make anxiety worse, so gradually facing them is often recommended.
GAD is a long-term condition, so the outlook is usually one of managing it over time.
note: NHS describes GAD as long-term; the outlook framing is ours.

sentence: Many people find that talking therapies, self-help and medicines help, though symptoms can return.

Where there is an immediate risk to life, call 999 or go to A&E.
Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 for anyone who needs someone to talk to.
NHS 111 mental health is not an emergency service, and it cannot arrange hospital admissions or give a diagnosis.
